items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "naval race".
items.answer: The Anglo-German competition to build battleships, especially Dreadnoughts, from 1906
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the Anglo-German competition to build battleships, especially Dreadnoughts, from 1906. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the Triple Entente and the Triple Alliance.
items.answer: The Triple Alliance (1882) linked Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy; the Triple Entente (completed 1907) was a looser understanding between Britain, France and Russia.
items.markingKey: The Triple Alliance (1882) linked Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy; the Triple Entente (completed 1907) was a looser understanding between Britain, France and Russia. items.stem: A student claims: "Only Germany wanted war in 1914." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Historians debate responsibility; decisions in Vienna, St Petersburg, Paris and London also contributed.
items.markingKey: Historians debate responsibility; decisions in Vienna, St Petersburg, Paris and London also contributed. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using the Second Moroccan Crisis (1911) as an example, explain imperial rivalry.
items.answer: Germany sent the gunboat Panther to Agadir to challenge French control; Britain backed France, and Germany backed down. Colonial disputes strengthened the Entente and increased German fears of encirclement.
items.markingKey: Context (Germany sent the gunboat Panther to Agadir to challenge French control; Britain backed France, and Germany backed down.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.answer: 19th century CE
items.markingKey: B. 1879 CE falls in the 19th century CE: e.g. the 15th century CE runs from 1401 to 1500.

items.answer: Weakness: it is too broad for a focused investigation Improved: "To what extent was the Anglo-German naval race responsible for Britain entering the First World War in 1914?"
items.markingKey: 1 mark: weakness identified (it is too broad for a focused investigation); 1-2 marks: a focused question such as "To what extent was the Anglo-German naval race responsible for Britain entering the First World War in 1914?" items.stem: You have three weeks to investigate "To what extent was the Anglo-German naval race responsible for Britain entering the First World War in 1914?" Outline a step-by-step plan, the sources you would use and one way you would evaluate your process at the end.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Militarism was the most important long-term cause of the First World War."
items.answer: Militarism made war more likely and harder to stop, but it interacted with alliances and nationalism; no single factor fully explains the outbreak.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: the naval and arms races created fear and mistrust; war plans like the Schlieffen Plan reduced time for diplomacy. Arguments against: alliances turned a Balkan dispute into a European war; nationalism in the Balkans created the crisis itself. Supported judgement: Militarism made war more likely and harder to stop, but it interacted with alliances and nationalism; no single factor fully explains the outbreak. items.stem: Briefly explain why Serbian nationalism threatened Austria-Hungary.
items.answer: Austria-Hungary was a multinational empire with many South Slavs; Serbian nationalism encouraged them to break away, threatening the empire's survival.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Austria-Hungary was a multinational empire with many South Slavs; Serbian nationalism encouraged them to break away, threatening the empire's survival. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "ultimatum".
items.answer: A final set of demands, with a threat of action if they are rejected; Austria-Hungary sent one to Serbia on 23 July 1914

items.answer: Germany's war plan required it to strike France before Russia was ready, so Russian mobilisation led Germany to declare war on Russia and France and invade Belgium.

items.answer: The assassination was a single event on 28 June; the July Crisis was the month of decisions by governments that turned it into a general war.

Fighting from systems of dug-in trenches, typical of the Western Front from late 1914 to 1918
The area between opposing front-line trenches
A former German or Ottoman territory administered by an Allied power under League of Nations supervision

items.markingKey: B. "trench warfare" is fighting from systems of dug-in trenches, typical of the Western Front from late 1914 to 1918.

items.stem: A student claims: "The First World War was fought only in Europe." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.

items.answer: Governments mobilised entire economies, conscripted men, directed industry, rationed food, used propaganda and drew women into the workforce, so civilians were fully involved.

items.stem: Plan an extended response to the question: "The experience of trench warfare has been exaggerated in popular memory." To what extent do you agree? Give a thesis, two arguments with specific evidence, a counter-argument and a conclusion.
items.answer: Thesis: Popular memory simplifies the experience, but the scale of suffering was real; historians argue that experiences varied widely by time, place and role.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: soldiers did not spend all their time in front-line trenches; many soldiers were not involved in major offensives. items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The term used during the war for the psychological trauma suffered by soldiers"?
items.answer: shell shock
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of shell shock.

items.stem: Outline one way in which the Brighton Pavilion hospital shows colonial soldiers' experiences.
items.answer: From 1914 to 1916 the Royal Pavilion in Brighton served as a hospital for wounded Indian soldiers, with separate kitchens for different dietary needs. It shows how the empire was visibly present on the British home front.

items.answer: Origin: Composite paraphrase of letters by Indian soldiers, 1915, from the censored mail extracts collected by the Indian Mail Censor (published in David Omissi, Indian Voices of the Great War, 1999). Limitation: Letters were censored, so soldiers may have avoided criticism; they were also often written by scribes.

items.stem: Rafael writes: "The Treaty of Versailles made Germany pay all of the 132 billion gold marks." Explain why this is inaccurate.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the Paris Peace Settlement and the Treaty of Versailles.
items.answer: Versailles was the treaty with Germany; the wider settlement also included Saint-Germain (Austria), Trianon (Hungary), Neuilly (Bulgaria) and Sèvres (Ottoman Empire).

items.stem: Outline one way in which the Ruhr occupation (1923) shows reactions to reparations.
items.answer: When Germany fell behind on reparations, French and Belgian troops occupied the Ruhr; German workers went on strike, and hyperinflation followed. Enforcing the treaty deepened German resentment and economic crisis.
items.markingKey: Context (When Germany fell behind on reparations, French and Belgian troops occupied the Ruhr; German workers went on strike, and hyperinflation followed.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Historians estimate that under the Treaty of Versailles Germany lost about 48% of its pre-war iron ore production. If pre-war iron ore production was about 28 million tonnes a year, calculate the approximate amount lost and explain why this loss mattered for Germany.
items.answer: about 13.4 million tonnes a year
items.markingKey: 48% × 28 = 13.4 (M1 A1). Explanation (2): e.g. loss of industrial resources weakened recovery and reparations capacity; losses fuelled resentment.

items.stem: Ingrid argues that "The Treaty of Versailles was too harsh on Germany." Sana disagrees. Explain one piece of evidence each student could use, and state which view you find more convincing and why.
items.answer: The treaty was harsh enough to cause bitter resentment but not harsh enough to permanently weaken Germany; its problems lay as much in enforcement as in its terms.
items.markingKey: Ingrid: reparations and war guilt caused lasting resentment. Sana: Germany's own treaty with Russia at Brest-Litovsk (1918) was harsher. items.stem: Explain why many Germans resented the Treaty of Versailles.

items.answer: the launch of HMS Dreadnought → the Bosnian Crisis → the First Balkan War → the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand
items.markingKey: the launch of HMS Dreadnought → the Bosnian Crisis → the First Balkan War → the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand. A larger BCE number is earlier. 2 marks all correct, 1 mark one adjacent pair swapped.

items.stem:
Source A – Book (paraphrased): Paraphrase of John Maynard Keynes, The Economic Consequences of the Peace, London, 1919

The author, an economist who had attended the conference, argued that the reparations demanded from Germany were far beyond its capacity to pay and that the treaty ignored the economic recovery of Europe. He predicted it would lead to economic disaster and political instability.

Outline the main argument or view that Source A presents, quoting or referring to the source.
items.answer: Reparations were excessive and would damage Europe.
items.markingKey: Reparations were excessive and would damage Europe. Award 1 mark per relevant point drawn from the source, up to [3]; own knowledge is not credited here. Criterion D: interpreting a source.

items.stem: Which of the following is the most clear and focused research question for an investigation into the July Crisis of 1914 and the outbreak of war?
options: How far did the German "blank cheque" of July 1914 determine Austria-Hungary's decision to declare war on Serbia?
items.answer: How far did the German "blank cheque" of July 1914 determine Austria-Hungary's decision to declare war on Serbia?
items.markingKey: C. It is open, has a clear scope (place/period/group) and can be answered with evidence; the others are too broad, closed or off-topic.

items.stem: Chloé argues that "The experience of trench warfare has been exaggerated in popular memory." Tariq disagrees. Explain one piece of evidence each student could use, and state which view you find more convincing and why.
items.answer: Popular memory simplifies the experience, but the scale of suffering was real; historians argue that experiences varied widely by time, place and role.
items.markingKey: Chloé: soldiers did not spend all their time in front-line trenches. Tariq: casualties on the Somme and at Verdun were enormous. Judgement (1-2 marks): Popular memory simplifies the experience, but the scale of suffering was real; historians argue that experiences varied widely by time, place and role.

items.stem:
Source A – Historian's interpretation (paraphrased): Paraphrase of Fritz Fischer, Griff nach der Weltmacht (Germany's Aims in the First World War), Düsseldorf, 1961

The historian argued that Germany's leaders deliberately pursued aggressive aims before 1914, seeking to dominate Europe and expand overseas, and that they used the July Crisis to launch a war they had long considered.

Using Source A and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim that "Militarism was the most important long-term cause of the First World War."
items.answer: Militarism made war more likely and harder to stop, but it interacted with alliances and nationalism; no single factor fully explains the outbreak.
items.markingKey: From the source: Germany bore primary responsibility because of its aggressive war aims. Own knowledge for: the naval and arms races created fear and mistrust; war plans like the Schlieffen Plan reduced time for diplomacy. Own knowledge against: alliances turned a Balkan dispute into a European war; nationalism in the Balkans created the crisis itself. Judgement: Militarism made war more likely and harder to stop, but it interacted with alliances and nationalism; no single factor fully explains the outbreak. Top answers integrate the source with own knowledge and comment on the source's origin/purpose. items.stem: "The Treaty of Versailles was too harsh on Germany." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: The treaty was harsh enough to cause bitter resentment but not harsh enough to permanently weaken Germany; its problems lay as much in enforcement as in its terms.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: reparations and war guilt caused lasting resentment; Germany lost 13% of its European territory and all its colonies. Arguments against: Germany's own treaty with Russia at Brest-Litovsk (1918) was harsher; Germany kept its unity and industry and reparations were later reduced. Supported judgement: The treaty was harsh enough to cause bitter resentment but not harsh enough to permanently weaken Germany; its problems lay as much in enforcement as in its terms. items.stem:
Source A – Historian's interpretation (paraphrased): Paraphrase of Christopher Clark, The Sleepwalkers: How Europe Went to War in 1914, London, 2012

The historian argued that the outbreak of war was not the result of one country's plan but of decisions by leaders in several capitals who were watchful but unseeing, blind to the full horror of the war they were bringing about.

Evaluate Source A as evidence about the July Crisis of 1914 and the outbreak of war. Consider its origin, purpose, value and limitations.
items.answer: Origin: Paraphrase of Christopher Clark, The Sleepwalkers: How Europe Went to War in 1914, London, 2012. Purpose: to re-examine the July Crisis from the perspectives of all the powers. Value: It draws on archives from many countries and challenges simple blame. Limitation: Critics argue it underplays German and Austro-Hungarian responsibility; it is one interpretation.

items.stem: Approximate estimates: Austria-Hungary mobilised 7.8 million men and lost 1.2 million killed; the United States mobilised 4.36 million and lost 0.13 million. Calculate the percentage killed for each and suggest two reasons why the figures differ.
items.answer: Austria-Hungary: 15.4%; the United States: 3.0%
items.markingKey: Austria-Hungary 15.4% (M1 A1); the United States 3.0% (A1). Reasons (2): length of involvement (the USA fought from 1917–18), fronts fought on, intensity of battles such as Verdun, medical care, and the reliability of records.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "imperialism"?
options: A strategy of wearing down the enemy through continual losses of soldiers and resources
The policy of extending a country's power by acquiring colonies or controlling other territories
The two rival blocs before 1914: the Triple Alliance (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy) and the Triple Entente (Britain, France, Russia)
Fighting from systems of dug-in trenches, typical of the Western Front from late 1914 to 1918
items.answer: The policy of extending a country's power by acquiring colonies or controlling other territories
items.markingKey: B. "imperialism" is the policy of extending a country's power by acquiring colonies or controlling other territories.

items.stem: In 1921 the Reparations Commission set Germany's reparations at what sum?
items.answer: 132 billion gold marks
items.markingKey: D. Much was never paid.

items.stem: Which event led Britain to declare war on Germany on 4 August 1914?
items.answer: Germany's invasion of Belgium
items.markingKey: A. Britain had guaranteed Belgian neutrality.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the Western Front and the Eastern Front.
items.answer: The Western Front in France and Belgium became a static line of trenches; the Eastern Front between Germany/Austria-Hungary and Russia was longer and more mobile.
items.markingKey: The Western Front in France and Belgium became a static line of trenches; the Eastern Front between Germany/Austria-Hungary and Russia was longer and more mobile. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why the alliance system turned a local conflict into a general European war.
items.answer: Commitments between the great powers meant that a dispute between Austria-Hungary and Serbia drew in Russia, then Germany, France and Britain, as each felt obliged or pressured to support its partner.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Commitments between the great powers meant that a dispute between Austria-Hungary and Serbia drew in Russia, then Germany, France and Britain, as each felt obliged or pressured to support its partner. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between the Paris Peace Settlement and the Treaty of Versailles.
items.answer: Versailles was the treaty with Germany; the wider settlement also included Saint-Germain (Austria), Trianon (Hungary), Neuilly (Bulgaria) and Sèvres (Ottoman Empire).
items.markingKey: Versailles was the treaty with Germany; the wider settlement also included Saint-Germain (Austria), Trianon (Hungary), Neuilly (Bulgaria) and Sèvres (Ottoman Empire). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between partial mobilisation and general mobilisation.
items.answer: Partial mobilisation prepares forces against one enemy; general mobilisation prepares the whole army, which other powers saw as a step towards war.
items.markingKey: Partial mobilisation prepares forces against one enemy; general mobilisation prepares the whole army, which other powers saw as a step towards war. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Soldiers spent all their time fighting at the front line." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Soldiers rotated between front-line, support and reserve trenches and rest areas; much time was spent on routine work, boredom and waiting.
items.markingKey: Soldiers rotated between front-line, support and reserve trenches and rest areas; much time was spent on routine work, boredom and waiting. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "The alliances legally forced every country to go to war in 1914." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The Entente was not a binding military alliance; Britain entered mainly over Germany's invasion of Belgium, and Italy stayed neutral despite the Triple Alliance.
items.markingKey: The Entente was not a binding military alliance; Britain entered mainly over Germany's invasion of Belgium, and Italy stayed neutral despite the Triple Alliance. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

Limitation: It focuses on German documents and may underplay the decisions of other powers; critics argued it read later aims back into 1914.

items.answer: France had lost about 1.4 million soldiers, its north-east had been devastated and it had been invaded twice in fifty years, so Clemenceau wanted to weaken Germany permanently and secure compensation.
